title: The Asymmetry of population ethics: experimental social choice and dual-process moral reasoning
venue: Economics and Philosophy 36(3) (2020); read as IZA Discussion Paper 12537 (August 2019), the version available to us

cost.compute_notes: Europe PMC full text for PMC11178026 returned an empty body (not open access via the API); the IZA working paper (40 pp, 68,168 chars) was read in full instead. No data or code located. Table 1 transcribed (artifacts/table1_transcribed.csv); counts reconstructed from shares and n and checked to round back. One script (reanalysis/a1.py), milliseconds.

triggers: is the procreation asymmetry intuitive to ordinary people
is a good life a reason to have a child according to lay people
share of inattentive or perverse answers in moral vignette surveys

claims.statement: Few respondents endorse the absolute Asymmetry: about three quarters say both a good and a bad expected life are moral reasons (for and against) a couple's having a child; the Asymmetry pattern (bad life relevant, good life irrelevant) is held by 12.5% (Study 1a) and 15.1% (Study 1b).
claims.scope: US MTurk, 2014-2015; Study 1a trichotomous relevance (n = 232), Study 1b nine-point scale (n = 186), within respondents, order of the two facts randomised; 10.1% of completers excluded for 'perverse' answers (e.g. a good life as a reason against).

quantities.name: share_both_additions_count
quantities.baseline: Study 1a: good and bad expected life both morally relevant (reasons framing)

quantities.name: share_procreation_asymmetry_mcmahan
quantities.baseline: Study 1a: bad life relevant, good life irrelevant

quantities.name: share_reverse_procreation_asymmetry
quantities.baseline: Study 1a: good life relevant, bad life irrelevant; Study 1b 3.2%

our_assessment.why: Table 1 is internally consistent (the printed marginals 78.9 / 86.6 and 78.0 / 89.8 are the sums of the cells within rounding). Accepted as a description of reasons-framed judgments. Note the exclusion rule: Spears drops the ~10% who answer in the 'wrong' direction; Caviola et al. (2022, Study 2a) keep their 11.5%, and in that study those respondents carry half of a reported effect. Two independent MTurk samples, two framings, the same ~10% rate of reversed answers -- a base rate worth carrying into any vignette study on procreation.

claims.statement: A quantitative asymmetry: across respondents assigned a life quality Q on a 0-10 ladder (Study 2), the probability that Q counts in favour rises less steeply over good lives than the probability that it counts against rises over bad lives (interaction t = 3.2, p < 0.01).
claims.scope: Study 2, MTurk 2015, Q randomised on 0-10, three-option response; linear-probability slopes compared. The author himself warns the comparison 'cannot be interpreted quantitatively literally'.

quantities.name: asymmetry_slope_interaction_t
quantities.n: not printed in the text read
quantities.baseline: slope of P(favour) on good lives vs slope of P(against) on bad lives

our_assessment.why: Comparing slopes of two bounded proportions over an ordinal ladder whose cardinal meaning respondents supply themselves is a scale-dependent comparison, and the author says so (Decancq et al.). Not checkable further without data. The robust part is qualitative and needs no slope comparison: good and even great lives count in favour, increasingly so (Q 8-10 above 6-7).

claims.statement: (Ours, cross-paper.) The Asymmetry is stronger when people judge REASONS for a procreative decision than when they judge whether an addition makes the WORLD better: here the Asymmetry pattern outnumbers its mirror image 57:17 (sign test p < 0.0001); in Caviola et al. 2022 Study 2a (world-betterness ratings) 12:10 (p = 0.83).
claims.scope: Spears Studies 1a+1b pooled (counts reconstructed from Table 1 shares) vs the type classification in caviola2022-population-ethical-intuitions#c3 (139 consistent responders). Different populations, years, wording and response formats.

our_assessment.why: Suggestive, not established, and tagged with the pattern it is most at risk of: Caviola's side has 22 discordant respondents, and the cross-study test is p = 0.058 with every design difference between the studies confounded with the framing. What it does is give a number to a conjecture Caviola et al. state in their own discussion (section 16.4: the asymmetry may live in deontic judgments, not axiological ones) and point at the decisive design: one sample, randomised to a reasons framing or a betterness framing, same scenario.

relations.why: Independent group, different instrument, same conclusion: the absolute Asymmetry is a minority view (12-15% here, 7.6% there); about three quarters count both good and bad lives. They disagree on the MIRROR (see c3 here), which is the more interesting fact.

One sample randomised between a reasons framing ('should this fact count for or against having the child?') and a betterness framing ('is the world better or worse?') with identical scenarios would decide c3. Neither group has run it.
